title: Orthogonal Persistance
section: 38. Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK
summary: Introduces orthogonal persistence: a canister can keep its variable state across redeploys without a database. A variable marked stable survives upgrades; a plain variable is reset. Demonstrated by redeploying with and without the stable keyword.

concepts.heading: What persistence means here
points: Normally, restarting or redeploying a program resets variables to their initial values; the earlier increments are lost. A JS demo makes this obvious: add 5 to a variable, remove that line, reload, and the value is back to the start.
To keep data across runs in ordinary software you need explicit persistence: a database, with code to write and read it.

On the Internet Computer a canister can retain its whole state (variables, collections, objects) automatically. It is called orthogonal because the developer does not have to write any storage code for it; it comes from the platform design.

concepts.heading: stable vs flexible variables
points: A normal `var` is a flexible variable and is reset on upgrade. Flexible is the default, matching other languages.
Prefix with `stable` to opt in: `stable var currentValue : Nat = 300;` Now the value survives redeploys and restarts, even downtime.
A stable declaration still has an initial value, used only the first time the canister is installed.

(Extra) The reference repo notes that in newer Motoko with `persistent actor`, variables are stable implicitly, so the explicit keyword triggers a redundant-stable warning (M0218). Type annotation `: Nat` is added in that code.

concepts.heading: Why the reassignment line must go
points: A statement like `currentValue := 100;` in the actor body runs every time the actor code is initialised (each deploy), overwriting whatever was restored.
To see persistence working, comment out that line. The declaration's initial value applies once; the replace operator would clobber it every time.

concepts.heading: Experiment to run
points: Without stable: deploy, query (300), topUp 100, query (400); change any line (e.g. add a Debug.print) and redeploy; query shows 300 again.
With stable: repeat the same steps; after redeploy the query still reports 400.
Use checkBalance (query) to read the value, and Candid UI to call topUp.

task.name: Observe orthogonal persistence
task.starting_point: DBank with topUp and checkBalance, currentValue starting at 300.
task.goal: See the balance reset on redeploy without stable, and survive with stable.
steps: Deploy, use Candid UI to topUp 100 and query: 400.
Make a trivial edit, redeploy, query again: back to 300.
Add the stable keyword to the variable declaration, deploy, topUp 100 (400).
Make another trivial edit, redeploy and query: still 400.
task.expected_result: Without stable the balance resets to 300; with stable it stays at 400 after redeploys.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 38 - Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK/38.06 Orthogonal Persistance/DBANK/src/DBANK/main.mo

pitfalls: Leaving the := reassignment in place, which resets the value on each run and hides the effect of stable.
Expecting non-stable vars to survive redeploys.
Forgetting that an initial value is only used on first install for stable variables.
(Extra) Changing a stable variable's type between deployments can need migration code; keep types compatible while experimenting.
